title: Hamiltonian Metric Learning and Energy-Based Training: A Dissipative Geometric Framework for Optimization
authors: Sparsho Chakraborty, Mohammad Alamgir, Nishanth M, Akshit Nanda, Ram Prasad Padhy, Sayan Mukherjee
abstract: Optimization in machine learning is usually expressed through iterative rules that update model parameters using information from the loss landscape. In this work, we study an alternative viewpoint in which parameter optimization is treated as the evolution of a dissipative dynamical system. The model parameters are regarded as generalized coordinates, the loss acts as a potential energy, and a positive-definite metric defines the local kinetic geometry of parameter space. Starting from a variational formulation, we derive the corresponding Hamiltonian dynamics, the geometric force generated by a position-dependent metric, and a metric-compatible Rayleigh dissipation law. The resulting continuous system satisfies a monotonic energy-dissipation relation, while its discrete form allows the influence of curvature on the optimization trajectory to be studied directly. We illustrate the framework using a controlled CIFAR-10 image-reconstruction problem for which the optimum is known analytically. With the image Hessian used as the metric, the curvature dependence of the quadratic modal dynamics is removed. We then reparameterize the same image as a matrix product state, producing a genuinely position-dependent metric and a nonzero geometric force. Poincaré return maps provide a complementary phase-space view of the resulting contraction dynamics. These examples establish HAMLET as a geometric, energy-based framework for studying optimization as dissipative motion in parameter space. On a five-seed MNIST MLP benchmark, HAMLET attains the highest mean test accuracy (97.95\%) and the lowest mean test negative log-likelihood (0.0696) among the three evaluated optimizers.
summary: This work develops HAMLET, a geometric framework that models machine learning optimization as a dissipative dynamical system. It treats the loss as potential energy and the parameter metric as kinetic geometry, deriving a full mechanical description. By analyzing controlled examples, the authors demonstrate how the metric induces a geometric force, providing a unified, physically rigorous view of optimization.
main_problem: The paper reframes machine learning parameter optimization from standard iterative rules into the framework of a dissipative dynamical system.
main_result: The proposed HAMLET framework successfully models optimization as a mechanical process governed by a Hamiltonian, a geometric force derived from the metric, and a dissipation term.
method: The authors derive the dynamics from a variational principle, leading to a continuous system that satisfies a monotonic energy-dissipation relation.
model_or_system: The model treats model parameters as generalized coordinates, the loss function as potential energy, and a positive-definite metric defining the local kinetic geometry of the parameter space.
key_observables: Poincaré return maps, geometric force ($F_{geo}$), energy dissipation rate, and mean test accuracy/negative log-likelihood on benchmarks.
important_parameters: The metric tensor $g(	heta)$, the loss function $L(	heta)$, and the dissipation coefficient $\gamma$.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that optimization can be viewed as the trajectory of a physically motivated dynamical system, requiring the metric and loss to be sufficiently smooth.
figures_summary: Figures compare Poincaré analysis for pixel space (constant metric) versus MPS space (position-dependent metric), showing how the geometric force and metric variation affect phase-space contraction.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the Hamiltonian/dissipative framework, derives the governing equations including the geometric force, illustrates this with controlled image reconstruction problems (pixel vs. MPS), and concludes with benchmark testing on MNIST.
why_interesting: The connection between geometric dynamics (Hamiltonian mechanics) and the optimization landscape provides a powerful, physically grounded lens for understanding deep learning training dynamics, which is relevant to understanding complex energy landscapes in many-body physics.

The total energy decreases as the trajectory approaches the stationary state, while kinetic energy becomes small near the minimum. This behavior is the discrete counterpart of the continuous dissipation law ˙H = −γpTg−1p ≤0.
